Few areas of biomedicine have generated as much public expectation as stem cell research, owing to the capacity of certain cells to differentiate into a wide range of specialised tissues and thereby, in principle, to repair organs damaged by injury or degenerative disease. The translation of this potential into approved treatments, however, has proved considerably slower than early enthusiasts predicted. At present, only a limited number of stem cell-based therapies, most notably bone marrow transplantation for certain blood disorders, are regarded as established medical practice. For the majority of other conditions, the evidence of safety and efficacy remains at the stage of early clinical trials.
This gap between expectation and evidence has been exploited by a growing number of private clinics in several countries, which market unproven stem cell injections directly to patients for conditions ranging from arthritis to multiple sclerosis. Such interventions are frequently administered without the controlled trials that regulatory agencies normally require. Moreover, a number of serious adverse events, including infections, tumour formation and loss of vision, have been documented in the medical literature. Patients, many of whom suffer from conditions for which conventional medicine offers little hope, may pay substantial sums for procedures whose benefits have never been demonstrated.
Regulators have responded in divergent ways. Some agencies have tightened their oversight, insisting that products involving substantial manipulation of cells be evaluated as medicines, while others have introduced accelerated approval pathways intended to speed patient access to promising therapies. Critics of the latter approach contend that lowering the evidential threshold risks legitimising treatments before their effectiveness has been established, whereas its supporters maintain that excessively rigid rules may deprive seriously ill patients of their only realistic options.

questions.passage:
It has become commonplace to attribute the apparent intensification of political polarisation in many democracies to the spread of social media, whose recommendation algorithms are said to confine users within so-called echo chambers in which they encounter only opinions that confirm their existing beliefs. Although intuitively persuasive, this account has received only partial support from empirical research. Large-scale analyses of online behaviour indicate that most users are in fact exposed to a more diverse range of news sources than the echo chamber hypothesis would predict. Strongly segregated information diets, by contrast, appear to be characteristic mainly of a relatively small, highly engaged minority.
Moreover, the chronology of polarisation complicates any simple causal explanation. In the United States, for instance, the divergence between the major parties was already well under way before the emergence of social networking platforms. Some studies have even reported that polarisation increased most rapidly among older citizens, the demographic group least likely to use such platforms. Experimental evidence is similarly mixed: in several studies, participants who temporarily deactivated their accounts reported modest reductions in hostility towards political opponents, whereas other experiments found that exposure to opposing views actually strengthened, rather than moderated, the original positions of participants.
None of this implies that social media are irrelevant. A more plausible interpretation, according to a number of political scientists, is that digital platforms amplify tendencies rooted in longer-term developments, such as the reorganisation of party coalitions, the fragmentation of traditional broadcasting and growing economic inequality. On this view, the principal effect of social media may be less to create divisions than to make existing ones more visible and emotionally charged, a distinction with considerable consequences for the design of effective policy responses.

questions.passage:
Along temperate coastlines, where mangroves cannot survive, salt marshes perform many of the same ecological functions. These grassy wetlands, which are flooded and drained by the tides twice a day, provide nursery grounds for fish, feeding areas for migrating birds and a natural buffer that absorbs the energy of waves during storms. They are also remarkably efficient at storing carbon: because their waterlogged soils contain little oxygen, plant material decomposes very slowly and can accumulate over centuries.
Despite these benefits, salt marshes have long been regarded as wasteland. Over the past few hundred years, large areas in Europe and North America were drained for agriculture, built on or enclosed behind sea walls. The walls themselves have created a further problem known as coastal squeeze. As sea levels rise, marshes would naturally migrate inland, but where a hard barrier blocks their path, they are gradually drowned and disappear.
In recent decades, some coastal authorities have begun to change their approach. Under a policy often described as managed realignment, old sea walls are deliberately breached or moved further inland, allowing the tide to flood former farmland so that new marshes can form. Supporters argue that such schemes can be cheaper in the long run than maintaining ever-higher defences. The policy is not without its difficulties, however. Landowners may be reluctant to give up productive fields, and newly created marshes often take decades to develop the full range of plants and animals found in natural ones. For this reason, many ecologists stress that restoring lost marshes is no substitute for protecting those that still exist.

questions.passage:
Bronze, an alloy made by combining copper with a small amount of tin, was harder than pure copper and could be cast into a wide variety of shapes, from axes and swords to ornaments and vessels. Its adoption, beginning in parts of western Asia around 3000 BC and spreading gradually across Europe and beyond, was so significant that nineteenth-century scholars named an entire period of prehistory after it. Yet the metal posed a puzzle that archaeologists are still working to solve. Copper deposits are fairly common, but tin is rare, and in many regions where bronze was widely used there were no local sources of it at all.
This scarcity meant that bronze production depended on trade networks that often stretched over very long distances. Chemical and isotopic analyses of tin ingots recovered from shipwrecks in the eastern Mediterranean, for example, suggest that some of the metal may have come from as far away as Cornwall in Britain or from deposits in Central Asia. Such findings indicate that communities separated by thousands of kilometres were linked, directly or through many intermediaries, by the exchange of metals.
Some historians argue that this dependence also made Bronze Age societies vulnerable. When trade routes were disrupted, as appears to have happened in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, palaces that controlled the supply of metal could lose much of their wealth and authority. Whether the disruption of the tin trade actually contributed to the collapse of several states at that time remains uncertain, since droughts, earthquakes and invasions have also been proposed as causes. It is notable, however, that iron, whose ores are found almost everywhere, became increasingly common in the centuries that followed.

questions.passage:
Bronze, an alloy made by combining copper with a small amount of tin, was harder than pure copper and could be cast into a wide variety of shapes, from axes and swords to ornaments and vessels. Its adoption, beginning in parts of western Asia around 3000 BC and spreading gradually across Europe and beyond, was so significant that nineteenth-century scholars named an entire period of prehistory after it. Yet the metal posed a puzzle that archaeologists are still working to solve. Copper deposits are fairly common, but tin is rare, and in many regions where bronze was widely used there were no local sources of it at all.
This scarcity meant that bronze production depended on trade networks that often stretched over very long distances. Chemical and isotopic analyses of tin ingots recovered from shipwrecks in the eastern Mediterranean, for example, suggest that some of the metal may have come from as far away as Cornwall in Britain or from deposits in Central Asia. Such findings indicate that communities separated by thousands of kilometres were linked, directly or through many intermediaries, by the exchange of metals.
Some historians argue that this dependence also made Bronze Age societies vulnerable. When trade routes were disrupted, as appears to have happened in the eastern Mediterranean around 1200 BC, palaces that controlled the supply of metal could lose much of their wealth and authority. Whether the disruption of the tin trade actually contributed to the collapse of several states at that time remains uncertain, since droughts, earthquakes and invasions have also been proposed as causes. It is notable, however, that iron, whose ores are found almost everywhere, became increasingly common in the centuries that followed.

options: show that iron was harder than bronze
explain how tin was extracted from its ores
argue that iron caused the droughts and earthquakes of 1200 BC
prove that palaces controlled the supply of iron
suggest that a metal with widely available ores was less dependent on long-distance trade

Demirin bronzdan ‘harder’ olduğu karşılaştırması, kalayın nasıl ‘extracted’ edildiği, demirin kuraklık ve depremlere ‘caused’ olduğu ve sarayların demir arzını ‘controlled’ ettiği metinde yer almaz.
